doc.title: Karl Berger interviewed by Monk Rowe, Woodstock, New York, August 11, 2014

chapter: Free jazz, time and the Creative Music Studio
title: Tune In, and Ed Blackwell playing without reading
summary: Audio excerpt from a Milestone album; Berger describes Blackwell, who never read music yet played every take differently, and compares Han Bennink.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: I have a couple of excerpts here that I wanted to ask you about. You guys have done so much music, I’m not sure you remember everything you did, but —
Yeah, that’s from the Milestone album.
So was this written out? That much of it? © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-
Because I know the tune comes back later.
Yeah, this is a tune called “Tune In.” So everybody has the melody. And Blackwell plays with his eyes closed so he doesn’t need any music.
I was just going to ask about that.

No, Blackwell doesn’t read. He never read. But he is so fast, like you know, you could write the most intricate pattern and he will play it and next time he’ll play a new version of it and everyone will be perfect. He was such a perfectionist in every way. But you could not pin him down on a pattern. You couldn’t tell Blackwell what to play. He would come up with the patterns. But every take would be a different pattern he would come up with. So he was like one of a kind. We just played in Berlin with a guy Han Bennink. He is a drummer. And he is sort of similar. He had that similar thing. Like when they gave him a chart he says, “I play with my eyes closed.” But he played perfect arrangements and the arrangement will always be slightly different every time he played it. So that’s sort of a talent that someone must have.
